meaning: Sudden and unexpected, often in a way that is jarring.
examples: The fossil record shows an [[abrupt]] rise in ocean temperatures about 56 million years ago.
partners: an abrupt change / shift / end / halt

lookalikes.tell: Abrupt means sudden; abridged means shortened.
Abrupt is an adjective meaning sudden; erupt is a verb meaning burst out.

meaning: To choose not to do or have something, especially not to vote or not to indulge in something.
short: choose not to do or take part
examples: Three delegates [[abstained]] from the vote, unwilling to support either proposal.

lookalikes.tell: To abstain is to hold back by choice; to be absent is simply not to be there.
Abstain means hold back from something; obtain means get it.

meaning: To make something more noticeable or prominent; to emphasize.
examples: The painter's use of deep shadow [[accentuates]] the lines of fatigue on the farmer's face.
partners: accentuate a feature / a contrast / the positive

lookalikes.tell: Accentuate makes something stronger or more noticeable; attenuate makes it weaker or thinner.
Accentuate is the verb for making something stand out; an accent is a mark or a way of speaking.

meaning: Severe and intense, as in an acute shortage or acute pain. Said of the senses or the mind, it means sharp and keen.
short: severe and intense; also sharp or keen
examples: The drought caused an [[acute]] shortage of drinking water across the region's farming towns.

lookalikes.tell: An acute problem is severe and often sudden; a chronic one drags on for a long time.
An acute shortage is a severe one; an astute person is shrewd and hard to fool.

meaning: Very skilled or good at something.
examples: Mendel proved [[adept]] at designing experiments that isolated a single trait at a time.

lookalikes.tell: Adept is an adjective meaning skilled; adopt is a verb meaning take up or take in.
Adept means skilled; adapt means adjust to new conditions.

meaning: Friendly, good-natured, and easy to talk to.
short: friendly and easy to talk to
examples: Though [[affable]] with visitors, the senator was known among her staff for her exacting standards.

lookalikes.tell: Affable describes a friendly person; affordable describes a reasonable price.
Affable means friendly; ineffable means too great to be put into words.

meaning: Having a great deal of money or wealth; prosperous.
examples: The study compared school funding in [[affluent]] suburbs with funding in low-income rural districts.

lookalikes.tell: Affluent means wealthy; effluent is liquid waste flowing out of a factory or plant.
Affluent is about wealth; fluent is about speaking or writing smoothly.

meaning: To set aside or hand out something, such as money, time, or resources, for a particular purpose.
short: set aside or distribute for a purpose
examples: The city council [[allocated]] a third of the new budget to repairing aging water pipes.

lookalikes.tell: Allocate means hand out for a purpose; locate means find.
Allocate means assign resources; relocate means move to a new place.

meaning: Showing unselfish concern for the well-being of others, even at a cost to oneself.
examples: Biologists long puzzled over [[altruistic]] behavior in animals, such as vampire bats sharing food with roost mates that are not their kin.

lookalikes.tell: Altruistic means unselfish; artistic means related to art.

meaning: Similar or comparable in some respect, so that one can help explain or understand the other.
examples: Early physicists described the atom as [[analogous]] to a tiny solar system, with electrons orbiting like planets.
partners: analogous to; an analogous case / situation

lookalikes.tell: Analogous means comparable to something else; anomalous means unlike the norm.
Analogous means comparable; analog describes a device that uses continuous signals, like a dial clock.

uses: In answer choices: "It describes a situation analogous to the one discussed in the first paragraph."

meaning: Providing support or help but not central; secondary to something more important.
examples: Beyond its main exhibits, the museum runs [[ancillary]] programs such as lectures and school workshops.

lookalikes.tell: Ancillary means supporting or secondary; ancestral means inherited from ancestors.

meaning: Strong dislike or hostility, often lasting a long time.
examples: Decades of [[animosity]] between the two ranching families erupted when the new fence went up.

lookalikes.tell: Animosity is hostility; animation is liveliness or moving images.
Animosity is hatred; equanimity is calm composure.

meaning: Having a name that is not known or not made public.
examples: The pamphlet was published by an [[anonymous]] author, and historians still debate who wrote it.

lookalikes.tell: Anonymous means unnamed; unanimous means everyone agrees.
Anonymous means without a known name; synonymous means having the same meaning.

meaning: Large or important enough to be noticed or measured.
short: large enough to notice or measure
examples: The new drug produced no [[appreciable]] improvement in patients over the six-month trial.

lookalikes.tell: Appreciable means noticeable in size; appreciative means grateful.
Appreciable means large enough to notice; applicable means relevant or usable in a case.

meaning: Exactly suitable or fitting for the situation, as in an apt comparison.
examples: Critics found the novel's title [[apt]]: its characters are all, in one way or another, strangers in their own homes.

lookalikes.tell: Apt means fitting; adept means skilled.
Apt means suitable; inept means clumsy or incompetent (inapt is the word for unsuitable).

meaning: To have a strong hope or ambition to achieve something.
examples: Like many young writers of her era, she [[aspired]] to publish in the national magazines of New York.
partners: aspire to a career / to become

lookalikes.tell: Aspire means aim for something yourself; inspire means move someone else to act or feel.
Aspire means aim high; expire means end or run out.

meaning: To make an unpleasant feeling, such as fear, guilt, or hunger, less intense.
examples: The company released its safety data in an effort to [[assuage]] the fears of nearby residents.

lookalikes.tell: Assuage means soothe a feeling; persuade means convince.

meaning: So surprising that it is hard to believe.
examples: The probe returned [[astonishing]] images of ice volcanoes on a moon once thought to be frozen solid.

lookalikes.tell: Astonishing describes the thing that surprises; astonished describes the person who is surprised.

meaning: Quick to notice and understand things, especially in a way that gives an advantage.
examples: An [[astute]] observer of politics, Tocqueville noticed tensions in American democracy that its own citizens overlooked.

lookalikes.tell: Astute means shrewd; acute usually means severe, as in an acute shortage.

meaning: Severely plain, with no decoration, luxury, or comfort. Of a person, it means stern and strict.
examples: The monks lived in [[austere]] cells furnished with only a cot, a stool and a candle.

lookalikes.tell: Austere is the adjective (plain, strict); austerity is the noun, often a government cutting its spending.
Austere means stern or plain; auspicious means promising good things to come.

meaning: Strongly disliking or unwilling to do something; usually followed by "to."
examples: Investors [[averse]] to risk tend to prefer government bonds over young technology firms.

lookalikes.tell: Averse describes a person who dislikes something; adverse describes conditions or effects that are harmful.

meaning: To prevent something bad from happening. It can also mean to turn one's eyes away.
examples: Quick action by air traffic controllers [[averted]] a collision over the crowded airport.

lookalikes.tell: Avert means head off something bad; divert means change the course or direction of something.
Avert is a verb meaning prevent; overt is an adjective meaning done openly.

meaning: Very eager and enthusiastic about something.
examples: An [[avid]] beetle collector, the young Darwin once put one in his mouth to free his hands for another.

lookalikes.tell: Avid means eager; vivid means bright or lifelike.
Avid means eager; arid means very dry.

meaning: So ordinary and overused that it is dull and unoriginal.
examples: Reviewers praised the actors but found the dialogue [[banal]], full of lines they had heard a hundred times.

lookalikes.tell: Banal means dull and trite; a bane is a cause of ruin or misery.
Banal means dull; venal means open to bribery.

meaning: Coming or happening later than it should have.
examples: Rosalind Franklin's part in discovering the structure of DNA received [[belated]] recognition long after her death.

lookalikes.tell: Belated means late; bloated means swollen.
Belated means overdue; berated means scolded angrily.

meaning: Very obvious and done openly, with no attempt to hide something bad.
examples: The judge called the contract a [[blatant]] attempt to get around the new labor law.

lookalikes.tell: Blatant means openly obvious; latent means present but hidden or not yet active.
Blatant means glaringly obvious; bland means mild and dull.

meaning: Hard but easily broken or cracked. Said of things like peace or confidence, it means fragile.
examples: Cold temperatures made the ship's steel hull [[brittle]], so it cracked instead of bending.

lookalikes.tell: Brittle means easily broken; a bristle is a stiff hair, and to bristle is to react angrily.

meaning: Cheerful and optimistic. Literally, able to stay afloat; said of an economy, rising and strong.
short: cheerful and upbeat; able to float
examples: Despite the poor harvest, the letters she sent home that autumn were [[buoyant]] and full of plans.
partners: a buoyant mood / buoyant spirits / a buoyant economy

lookalikes.tell: Buoyant is the adjective (cheerful, or floating); a buoy is a floating marker, and to buoy is to lift up.

meaning: To persuade someone to do something through flattery, gentle pressure, or repeated coaxing.
examples: The organizers [[cajoled]] reluctant local merchants into sponsoring the town's first public library.

lookalikes.tell: Cajole means win someone over with flattery; coerce means force them with threats.

meaning: Showing an insensitive, cruel disregard for other people's feelings or suffering.
examples: Reformers condemned the mill owners' [[callous]] indifference to the children working their looms.

lookalikes.tell: Callous means unfeeling; a callus is a patch of hardened skin.

meaning: The quality of being open and honest in what one says, even when the truth is unwelcome.
examples: Historians value the general's letters for their [[candor]] about the army's early defeats.

lookalikes.tell: Candor is the noun (honesty); candid is the adjective (honest and direct).

meaning: To cause or speed up a process or change. In chemistry, to speed up a reaction without being used up.
short: spark or speed up a change
examples: The publication of the report [[catalyzed]] a nationwide movement to clean up the rivers.

lookalikes.tell: Catalyze means spark or speed up a change; analyze means examine closely.
Catalyze means set a change in motion; catalog means make a list of items.

meaning: To give up control of something, such as land, power, or a point in an argument, often unwillingly.
short: give up (land, power, or a point)
examples: Under the 1848 treaty, Mexico [[ceded]] a vast northern territory to the United States.

lookalikes.tell: Cede means hand something over; secede means formally withdraw from a nation or group.
Cede means give up; seed means plant, or a plant's seed.

meaning: Relying on thought and reason rather than emotion or feeling; intellectual.
examples: Her early poems are [[cerebral]] puzzles; only in later collections does she write openly about grief.

lookalikes.tell: Cerebral describes a thinking-based style; erudite describes a person with deep learning from study.

meaning: To think deeply and carefully about something.
examples: The philosopher would [[cogitate]] on a single question for weeks before writing a word.

lookalikes.tell: Cogitate means think deeply; agitate means stir up or disturb.
Cogitate is the verb for thinking hard; cognition is the mental process of knowing.

meaning: Secret cooperation between people or groups to cheat, deceive, or do something illegal.
examples: Investigators found evidence of [[collusion]] among the three railroads, which had quietly agreed to fix their prices.

lookalikes.tell: Collusion is secret cooperation; a collision is a crash.
Collaboration is working together openly; collusion is working together secretly for a dishonest end.

meaning: Found or happening everywhere; ordinary and not unusual.
examples: Telephones, a rarity in American homes in 1900, were [[commonplace]] by the 1950s.

lookalikes.tell: Commonplace means ordinary and widespread; a commonality is a feature that things share.

meaning: Feeling or showing sympathy for others' suffering, together with a wish to help.
examples: Whitman's [[compassionate]] visits to wounded soldiers in Washington's hospitals shaped the poems of Drum-Taps.

lookalikes.tell: Compassionate means feeling for others' suffering; passionate means feeling strong emotion or enthusiasm of any kind.

meaning: Too satisfied with oneself or the situation, so that one fails to notice dangers or the need to improve.
examples: After years without a major flood, the town grew [[complacent]] and let the levees fall into disrepair.

lookalikes.tell: Complacent means smugly satisfied; complaisant means eager to please others.
Complacent means too satisfied to act; compliant means willing to obey.

meaning: Willing to obey rules, requests, or orders; also, meeting the standards that are required.
examples: Engineers had to make the old bridge [[compliant]] with the new earthquake codes.

lookalikes.tell: Compliant means obedient; a complaint is an expression of dissatisfaction.
Compliant means willing to follow rules; complacent means smugly unconcerned.

meaning: Having to do with ideas or concepts rather than concrete things or practical experience.
short: based on ideas rather than things
examples: The team's early work was purely [[conceptual]]; no one had yet built even a small working model.
partners: a conceptual framework / model; conceptual art

lookalikes.tell: Conceptual is about ideas; perceptual is about what the senses take in.
Conceptual concerns ideas; contextual concerns the surrounding circumstances.

meaning: Planned and carried out jointly, or done with great, determined effort.
examples: A [[concerted]] effort by farmers, scientists and state officials helped bring the whooping crane back from near extinction.

lookalikes.tell: Concerted means coordinated; disconcerted means unsettled or flustered.
Concerted means joint and coordinated; a concert is a musical performance (though "in concert" means together).

meaning: To accept or overlook behavior that is wrong, as if it were acceptable.
examples: The editorial argued that staying silent about the abuses amounted to [[condoning]] them.

lookalikes.tell: Condone means accept bad behavior; condemn means strongly disapprove of it.
Condone means excuse wrongdoing; condole means express sympathy.

uses: In answer choices: "The author neither condones nor condemns the character's decision to leave."

meaning: To protect something from harm, loss, or waste, or to use it carefully so that it lasts.
examples: During the drought, residents were asked to [[conserve]] water by watering their lawns only one day a week.

lookalikes.tell: Conserve means save; converse means talk, or the opposite of something.
Conserve means protect from waste; conservative describes preferring tradition or caution.

meaning: Helpful and intended to improve something, rather than to attack or tear it down.
examples: The reviewers' comments were sharp but [[constructive]], and each came with a suggestion for a better experiment.

lookalikes.tell: Constructive means helping to improve; instructive means teaching something useful.
Constructive means helpful; constrictive means tight or confining.

meaning: To challenge or argue against a claim, decision, or result, saying that it is wrong.
examples: Several historians [[contest]] the traditional date of the manuscript, arguing that its paper was made decades later.
partners: contest a claim / a decision / the results

lookalikes.tell: Contest as a verb means dispute; context means the surrounding circumstances.
To contest is to formally dispute a claim or result; to protest is to voice an objection, often publicly.

uses: In answer choices: "It contests the claim that the painting was finished before 1650."

meaning: Made to look exactly like something valuable or official in order to deceive; fake.
examples: By the end of the Civil War, so much [[counterfeit]] money was circulating that the federal government created the Secret Service in 1865 to fight it.

lookalikes.tell: Counterfeit means fake; a counterpart is a person or thing that matches another in a different setting.
Counterfeit means forged; forfeit means lose something as a penalty.

meaning: Having the opposite of the intended effect, so that it makes a problem worse.
examples: Harsh punishments proved [[counterproductive]]: students who were suspended fell even further behind.

lookalikes.tell: Unproductive means achieving little; counterproductive means actually working against the goal.
Counterproductive means backfiring; counterintuitive means contrary to what common sense expects.

meaning: Secret or hidden; not openly shown, done, or admitted.
examples: The Underground Railroad depended on [[covert]] networks of safe houses and coded messages.

lookalikes.tell: Covert means hidden; overt means openly shown.
Covert means secret; convert means change, or a person who has changed beliefs.

meaning: Too ready to believe things, even with little or no evidence.
examples: Tales of sea serpents found a [[credulous]] audience among readers who had never seen the ocean.

lookalikes.tell: Credulous describes a person who believes too easily; credible describes a claim or source that deserves belief.
Credulous means believing too easily; incredulous means unwilling or unable to believe.

meaning: To reach a final, highest point or result; usually followed by "in."
examples: Years of marches and court battles [[culminated]] in the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

lookalikes.tell: Culminate means reach a peak or end point; accumulate means build up over time.
Culminate means reach a climax; fulminate means protest angrily.

meaning: To make someone feel afraid or discouraged, especially about facing a difficult task.
examples: The steep, icy walls of the gorge did not [[daunt]] the survey team, who spent a month mapping them.

lookalikes.tell: Daunt means discourage or intimidate; taunt means mock or tease.
Daunt means discourage; vaunt means boast about.

meaning: To take something away from someone, or to keep them from having something they need or want.
short: take away or deny something needed
examples: The blockade [[deprived]] the city of grain for nearly two years.

lookalikes.tell: Deprive means take away; derive means obtain from a source.
Deprive means take away; depraved means morally corrupt.

meaning: Not emotionally involved; standing apart and viewing things calmly or objectively.
examples: The narrator describes the battle in a [[detached]] voice, as if reporting the weather.

lookalikes.tell: Detached means emotionally distant; detailed means full of particulars.
Detached means standing apart emotionally; attached means fond of or connected to.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator describes the events in a detached, almost clinical tone."

meaning: To spread out over a wide area or among many people. As an adjective, it means spread out and not concentrated.
examples: New farming techniques [[diffused]] slowly from village to village along the river valley.

lookalikes.tell: Diffuse means spread out; defuse means calm a tense situation or disarm a bomb.

meaning: To move away from the main subject for a while when speaking or writing.
examples: The essay [[digresses]] into a story about the author's grandfather before returning to its argument about farm policy.

lookalikes.tell: Digress means wander off the topic; regress means go back to an earlier, often worse, state.
Digress means stray from the point; digest means absorb food or information.

uses: In answer choices: "The author digresses to describe her own first visit to the site."

meaning: Not in agreement or harmony; clashing, whether in opinions, findings, or sounds.
examples: The two surveys produced [[discordant]] results, one showing the lake's fish population rising and the other showing it falling.

lookalikes.tell: Discordant means clashing or disagreeing; disconcerting means unsettling.

meaning: Not sincere or candid, especially by pretending to know less, or to be more honest, than one really is.
examples: Critics called the company's claim that it had never studied the risks [[disingenuous]], since its own scientists had warned of them for years.

lookalikes.tell: Ingenuous means innocent and trusting; disingenuous means only pretending to be.
Disingenuous means insincere; ingenious means clever and inventive.

uses: In answer choices: "The author suggests that the official's surprise at the report was disingenuous."

meaning: Gloomy and depressing; also, very poor in quality or result.
examples: After a [[dismal]] potato harvest in 1846, tens of thousands of families left Ireland for North America.

lookalikes.tell: Dismal means gloomy; a dismissal is a sending away or firing.
Dismal describes something gloomy; dismayed describes a person upset by something unexpected.

meaning: To scatter and fade away gradually until gone, as fog, heat, or tension does. It can also mean to waste money or energy foolishly.
examples: By midmorning the fog had [[dissipated]], revealing the ridge the hikers had been aiming for.
partners: tension / fog / heat dissipates; dissipate energy

lookalikes.tell: Dissipate means scatter until gone; disseminate means spread information widely on purpose.

meaning: Moving apart or differing from one another, as opinions, paths, or results can.
examples: The two populations of finches, separated for thousands of years, developed [[divergent]] beak shapes.

lookalikes.tell: Divergent means moving apart from one another; diverse means varied, made up of many kinds.
Divergent is a neutral word for differing; deviant describes departing from accepted norms, usually disapprovingly.

meaning: To make known something private or secret.
examples: The reporter refused to [[divulge]] the names of the officials who had given her the documents.

lookalikes.tell: Divulge means reveal; diverge means move apart.
Divulge means reveal a secret; indulge means allow oneself a pleasure.

meaning: Stating opinions as if they were certainly true, and refusing to consider other views or evidence.
short: rigidly insisting one's views are right
examples: The young astronomer found her [[dogmatic]] professor unwilling even to look at the new measurements.

lookalikes.tell: Dogmatic means rigidly sure of one's beliefs; pragmatic means focused on what works in practice.
Dogmatic means unbending in opinion; dramatic means striking or theatrical.

uses: In answer choices: "The critic's tone is dogmatic, allowing no room for other readings of the poem."

meaning: Unusual or strange in behavior or appearance, often in a harmless or charming way.
examples: Neighbors thought the [[eccentric]] inventor odd for flying kites in thunderstorms, but his notebooks were full of careful measurements.

lookalikes.tell: Eccentric means odd or unconventional; egocentric means self-centered.
Eccentric people are unusual; concentric circles share the same center.

meaning: Using money, time, or materials carefully and without waste.
examples: The new engine was far more [[economical]], running twice as long on the same tank of fuel.

lookalikes.tell: Economic means having to do with the economy; economical means saving money or resources.

meaning: Producing the desired result; effective, especially of a treatment or method.
examples: Early trials suggested that the vaccine was [[efficacious]] in adults but had not yet been tested in children.

lookalikes.tell: Efficacious means it works; efficient means it works without wasting time or resources.
Efficacious means effective; effusive means gushing with feeling.

meaning: To make a story or account more interesting by adding details that are often exaggerated or untrue. It can also mean to decorate.
examples: Historians suspect that the explorer [[embellished]] his journals, since no one else on the voyage recorded the giant sea turtles he described.
partners: embellish a story / an account / the truth

lookalikes.tell: Embellish means add flourishes to a story; embezzle means steal money one was trusted to manage.

meaning: Famous and highly respected within a particular field.
examples: The [[eminent]] geologist Charles Lyell urged the young Darwin to publish his theory before someone else did.

lookalikes.tell: Eminent means famous; imminent means about to happen.
Eminent means distinguished; immanent means existing within something.

meaning: Expressed with force and clarity, leaving no doubt; also, very clear and definite, as in an emphatic victory.
examples: Her reply was [[emphatic]]: the committee would not approve the dam without a full environmental study.

lookalikes.tell: Emphatic means forceful; empathetic means able to share others' feelings.

uses: In answer choices: "The author's emphatic rejection of the proposal leaves no room for compromise."

meaning: So absorbed in something that one pays no attention to anything else.
examples: [[Engrossed]] in the letters she had found in the attic, Nell did not hear the train pass.
partners: engrossed in a book / task / conversation

lookalikes.tell: Engrossed means deeply absorbed; engorged means swollen with blood or fluid.

meaning: So firmly established that it is very difficult to change or remove.
short: firmly fixed and hard to change
examples: Reformers found that the practice was [[entrenched]] in the city's hiring rules and would take a generation to undo.

lookalikes.tell: Entrenched means firmly established; trenchant means sharp and forceful, as in trenchant criticism.
Entrenched means firmly fixed; enriched means improved by adding something.

meaning: To name things one by one, as in a list.
examples: The Declaration of Independence [[enumerates]] the colonists' grievances against the king in a long series of charges.

lookalikes.tell: Enumerate means list; enunciate means pronounce clearly or state formally.
Enumerate means list one by one; numerate means able to work with numbers.

uses: In answer choices: "It enumerates the steps the researchers took to rule out contamination."

meaning: Happening at irregular intervals rather than continuously; also, made up of a series of separate episodes.
short: occurring now and then; in episodes
examples: The patient's symptoms were [[episodic]], flaring for a few days and then vanishing for months.
partners: episodic flooding / symptoms; an episodic novel

lookalikes.tell: Episodic means happening now and then; an epidemic is a widespread outbreak of disease.
Episodic describes something told or happening in separate parts; epic describes something grand and heroic in scale.

meaning: To be a perfect or typical example of something.
examples: For many readers, the lighthouse keeper's solitary life [[epitomizes]] the novel's theme of devotion.
partners: epitomize a quality / an era / a style

lookalikes.tell: To epitomize is to be the perfect example; an epitaph is words written on a tomb.
Epitomize is a verb; an epithet is a descriptive name or an insulting word.

uses: In answer choices: "The anecdote epitomizes the researcher's patience."

meaning: Fair and reasonable, treating everyone in a way that is just.
examples: The committee sought an [[equitable]] way to divide the river's water among farms both upstream and down.

lookalikes.tell: Equitable means fair; equable means even-tempered or steady, as in an equable climate.
Equitable means fair; equivalent means equal in value or meaning.

meaning: To destroy or remove something completely, so that it no longer exists.
examples: A worldwide vaccination campaign [[eradicated]] smallpox by 1980.
partners: eradicate a disease / poverty / a pest

lookalikes.tell: Eradicate means wipe out; irradiate means expose to radiation.
Eradicate means remove completely; radiate means spread out from a center.

meaning: Not regular, steady, or predictable in movement, behavior, or pattern.
examples: The satellite's [[erratic]] signal suggested that one of its antennas had been damaged.

lookalikes.tell: Erratic means irregular; errant means straying from the right course or behaving wrongly.
Erratic means unpredictable; erroneous means wrong.

meaning: To cause someone to become unfriendly or distant toward a person or group they were once close to.
examples: The long quarrel over the will [[estranged]] the two sisters for nearly twenty years.

lookalikes.tell: To estrange is to drive people apart; strange means odd or unfamiliar.

meaning: To escape or avoid something, such as a question, a duty, or a pursuer, especially by cleverness or trickery.
examples: The senator [[evaded]] the reporter's question by talking about the weather in her home state.
partners: evade a question / capture / taxes / responsibility

lookalikes.tell: Evade means avoid; invade means enter by force.

meaning: Vanishing quickly; lasting only a very short time.
examples: The poem captures the [[evanescent]] colors of a winter sunset, gone before the speaker can name them.

lookalikes.tell: Evanescent means quickly vanishing; effervescent means bubbly or lively.
Evanescent means fading fast; iridescent means shimmering with changing colors.

meaning: To cut out or remove something completely, such as a passage from a text or tissue from the body.
examples: The editor [[excised]] three chapters from the memoir, judging them too harsh toward living people.
partners: excise a passage / a scene / a tumor

lookalikes.tell: Excise means cut out; exercise means use or train.
Excise means cut out; exorcise means drive out an evil spirit.

meaning: Convenient and useful for a particular purpose, often even though it is not fair, principled, or wise in the long run.
examples: Abandoning the treaty was politically [[expedient]] but, the author argues, cost the nation its credibility.

lookalikes.tell: Expedient means convenient, often at the cost of principle; expeditious means quick and efficient.
Expedient is an adjective about convenience; expedite is a verb meaning speed something up.

meaning: To make a process happen more quickly or easily.
examples: A new rule [[expedited]] the review of drugs for rare diseases, cutting the wait by nearly a year.

lookalikes.tell: Expedite is a verb meaning speed up; expedient is an adjective meaning convenient.
Expedite means speed up; an expedition is a journey with a purpose.

meaning: To explain an idea or a text in detail, making its meaning clear.
examples: In her lectures, the critic [[explicates]] a single sonnet line by line for an entire hour.
partners: explicate a text / a theory / a poem

lookalikes.tell: Explicate is a verb meaning explain in detail; explicit is an adjective meaning stated clearly.
Explicate means explain; extricate means free from a difficulty.

uses: In answer choices: "It explicates a key term that the author uses throughout the passage."

meaning: Not relevant or essential to the matter at hand; also, coming from outside.
examples: The editor cut every [[extraneous]] detail until the story ran barely two pages.

lookalikes.tell: Extraneous means not relevant; extemporaneous means spoken without preparation.
Both can mean coming from outside, but extraneous stresses that something does not belong, while extrinsic stresses that it is not part of a thing's own nature.

meaning: Spending or using much more than is necessary or reasonable; also, going beyond what is reasonable, as in extravagant claims.
examples: The duke's [[extravagant]] parties drained a fortune that had taken three generations to build.

lookalikes.tell: Extravagant means too costly or excessive; extraneous means irrelevant.

meaning: Coming from outside something rather than being part of its own nature.
examples: Psychologists compare [[extrinsic]] rewards, such as grades and prizes, with the satisfaction a task brings on its own.

lookalikes.tell: Extrinsic means coming from outside; intrinsic means belonging to a thing's own nature.
Extrinsic means external; extinct means no longer existing.

meaning: Joking or trying to be funny at an inappropriate time, especially about a serious subject.
examples: His [[facetious]] remark about the flood struck the residents who had lost their homes as cruel.

lookalikes.tell: Facetious means joking; fictitious means made up.
Facetious means joking; factious means split into quarreling groups.

uses: In answer choices: "The author's facetious suggestion that the city simply ban winter is meant to mock the proposal."

meaning: Too simple; reached too easily, without careful thought about a complex issue. It can also mean done with ease.
examples: The reviewer dismissed the book's [[facile]] conclusion that poverty is caused by laziness alone.

lookalikes.tell: Facile means too simple; facilitate means make easier.

uses: In answer choices: "The author rejects the facile explanation offered by earlier critics."

meaning: Barely noticeable to the senses or the mind; weak or slight.
